raw_case_text: A 5-year-old boy with steroid dependent MCNS was admitted to our hospital. He has been treated with prednisone, cyclosporine and 9 consecutive intravenous pulses of cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2 monthly) in the past 3 years. However, the patient still relapsed frequently. Therefore, a single dose of rituximab (375 mg/m2) was given intravenously in the latest episode of relapse. Three days later, the number of CD20 positive B cell decreased to be 0.19%. The urine protein turned to be negative within 1 week. Unfortunately, the patient presented with high fever (39 C) and cough on Day 13 after rituximab treatment. The complete blood count (CBC) test showed that leukocytes 4.76 x 109/L, hemoglobin 136.0 g/L, platelets 333.0 x 109/L, neutrophil percentage 91%, C-reactive protein 6 mg/L. Serum albumin 36.65 g/L, globulin 18 g/L, sodium 140 g/L, potassium 4.5 g/L, calcium 2.06 g/L. Liver and renal function was normal. Urinalysis: urinary protein ++. The chest CT showed ground-glass opacities in both lungs (Figure 1C). mNGS showed there was pneumocystis carinii in bronchoalveolar lavage fluid. However, it was negative in sputum culture at the same time. Anti-infective treatment with meropenem, amoxicillin clavulanate potassium, oral SMZ-TMP and caspofungin were given. Meanwhile, the patient received mechanical ventilation due to severe respiratory distress. After 20 days of the treatment, dyspnea disappeared and the sign of lung infection was greatly improved (Figure 1D). Two months after RTX treatment, prednisone was terminated. One week after anti-PCP treatment, urinary protein turned to be negative. Moreover, the patient achieved complete remission in the following 24 months. The percentage of CD20 positive B cells were 2.6%, 5.9%, 16.1%, 24.2% in the 3rd, 6th, 12th and 24th month respectively.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 5-year-old boy with frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome presented with high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress 13 days after receiving a single dose of intravenous rituximab.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 3 years, the patient had been treated for steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) with oral prednisone, cyclosporine, and nine monthly pulses of intravenous cyclophosphamide (0.5 g/m2), but continued to relapse frequently. During his latest relapse, he received a single intravenous infusion of rituximab (375 mg/m2), which reduced his CD20+ B cells to 0.19% in 3 days and cleared his proteinuria within 1 week. On day 13 post-rituximab, he acutely developed high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress.
subjective.past_medical_history: Steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome (MCNS) treated over 3 years with prednisone, cyclosporine, 9 monthly IV cyclophosphamide pulses, and a single dose of IV rituximab 13 days prior.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high fever (39 °C), cough, and severe respiratory distress/dyspnea.

objective.physical_examination: High fever (39.0 °C) and severe respiratory distress requiring endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation.
objective.routine_investigations: Day 13 post-rituximab laboratory tests: WBC 4.76 x 10^9/L (91% neutrophils), hemoglobin 136.0 g/L, platelets 333.0 x 10^9/L, C-reactive protein (CRP) 6 mg/L, serum albumin 36.65 g/L, globulin 18 g/L, sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, calcium 2.06 mmol/L, normal hepatic and renal function, and urinalysis showing 2+ proteinuria; sputum culture negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Peripheral B-cell monitoring: CD20+ B cells decreased to 0.19% on day 3 post-rituximab (recovering to 2.6%, 5.9%, 16.1%, and 24.2% at months 3, 6, 12, and 24). Chest CT (day 13 post-rituximab): Bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS): Positive for Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Severe Pneumocystis carinii (jirovecii) pneumonia (PCP; confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage fluid mNGS and bilateral ground-glass opacities on chest CT despite negative sputum culture) presenting 13 days after single-dose rituximab in a 5-year-old boy with steroid-dependent minimal change nephrotic syndrome. Plan and clinical course: Treated with invasive mechanical ventilation, oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (SMZ-TMP), intravenous caspofungin, meropenem, and amoxicillin-clavulanate for 20 days, resulting in complete resolution of dyspnea and radiographic infiltrates. Urine protein turned negative 1 week after anti-PCP therapy, oral prednisone was discontinued 2 months post-rituximab, and he maintained complete nephrotic remission over 24 months of follow-up.
